This would not be a permanent division but a temporary stabilization mechanism, allowing both powers to focus on internal development rather than endless rivalry.

IV. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

A. "A New Yalta Would Legitimize Chinese Expansionism!"

Rebuttal:

  • China is already expanding—without a formal agreement, it does so unilaterally, leading to resistance (e.g., Taiwan, South China Sea).
  • A New Yalta would set clear rules: China gets East Asia, but not the Pacific Islands (U.S. sphere); the U.S. gets Europe, but not Chinese military bases in Africa.
  • Without it, China will keep pushing—leading to war, not stability.

B. "The U.S. Would Never Accept Chinese Dominance in Asia!"

Rebuttal:

  • The U.S. already accepts Chinese dominance in Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan (eventually)—it just refuses to acknowledge it publicly.
  • A New Yalta would formalize this reality, preventing miscalculations (e.g., U.S. "accidentally" bombing a Chinese ship in the Taiwan Strait).
  • The alternative is endless containment, which fails (see: Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq).

C. "This Would Be a Return to 19th-Century Imperialism!"

Rebuttal:

  • Imperialism was about conquest; a New Yalta would be about mutual recognition.
  • The alternative is chaos—where no nation has clear boundaries, leading to endless wars (Ukraine, Yemen, Syria).
  • Even the EU operates on spheres—Germany dominates Central Europe, France leads West Africa, Russia controls Belarus. The world has always had spheres—let’s make them explicit.

V. How a New Yalta Could Be Implemented

Step 1: Bilateral Negotiations (U.S.-China Track II Dialogues)

  • Think tanks (CSIS, Brookings, China’s CICIR) draft proposals.
  • Backchannel talks between Henry Kissinger (U.S.) and Yang Jiechi (China) could lay groundwork.

Step 2: A Formal Declaration (Like Yalta 1945)

  • Both leaders (Biden & Xi) announce a "21st Century Stability Pact" at a summit (e.g., Bali G20, APEC).
  • Key provisions:
    • U.S. recognizes China’s leadership in East Asia (including Taiwan’s eventual reunification).
    • China recognizes U.S. dominance in the Americas and Europe.
    • Neutral zones (e.g., Africa, Middle East) where both compete but avoid direct conflict.
    • Economic guarantees: No tariffs, no tech wars, stable supply chains.

Step 3: Regional Agreements to Enforce the Pact

  • East Asia: A Quad+China security framework (U.S., Japan, Australia, India, China) to prevent Taiwan conflict.
  • Europe: NATO-China non-aggression pact (China stays out of Eastern Europe; U.S. stays out of Central Asia).
  • Africa & Latin America: Debt-for-stability deals (China reduces BRI loans in exchange for no U.S. military bases).

Step 4: Enforcement Mechanisms

  • Joint crisis hotlines (like the U.S.-China military hotline) to prevent accidental wars.
  • Economic sanctions for violations (e.g., if China invades Taiwan, U.S. imposes full decoupling).
  • Periodic reviews (every 5-10 years) to adjust spheres as power shifts.

Conclusion: A New Yalta is the Only Path to Avoid Catastrophe

The world is not heading toward a peaceful coexistence—it is sleepwalking toward conflict. The U.S. and China are too powerful to fight directly, but too competitive to coexist without rules. A New Yalta is not a surrender to Chinese hegemony—it is a realistic acknowledgment of power realities that prevents war.

The alternatives are worse:

  • Uncontrolled rivalry → Taiwan War → Nuclear Exchange → Global Depression.
  • Endless containment → Proxy wars everywhere → Economic collapse.
  • Decoupling → Two separate blocs → Cold War 2.0 (but hotter).

A New Yalta would: ✅ Prevent direct war by defining clear boundaries. ✅ Stabilize trade by ending economic warfare. ✅ Reduce proxy conflicts by giving each side legitimate spheres. ✅ Preserve global order by replacing uncertainty with rules.

The Cold War ended because the U.S. and USSR accepted a spheres system—even if imperfect. The 21st century demands the same. The question is not whether the U.S. and China will divide the world—but how. The choice is between a negotiated New Yalta or a catastrophic war. History will judge which path was wiser.

The time to act is now. Before the next crisis forces an uncontrolled collision. Before miscalculation leads to war. A New Yalta is not a defeat—it is the only way to avoid annihilation.

Major Challenges & Why It’s Unlikely

Despite the theoretical benefits, several structural and ideological obstacles make such an agreement highly improbable:

  3. Taiwan as a Wild Card

    • Taiwan is non-negotiable for China (it sees it as a core sovereignty issue).
    • The U.S. cannot abandon Taiwan without undermining its credibility in Asia and encouraging other separatist movements (e.g., Tibet, Xinjiang).

  4. Domestic Politics in Both Countries

    • U.S.: Any deal perceived as "surrendering" to China would face strong bipartisan opposition (e.g., hawkish Republicans, Democratic progressives).
    • China: Xi Jinping’s regime needs external threats to justify its rule—a formalized division might reduce tensions and weaken its legitimacy.

  5. Lack of Trust & Historical Grievances

    • The U.S. views China as a strategic competitor (not just a rival but a long-term threat).
    • China sees the U.S. as containment-focused (e.g., "Pivot to Asia," sanctions, tech wars).
    • No mutual security guarantees exist—both sides would fear the other breaking the deal.

  6. Third-Party Resistance

    • Europe, India, Japan, Australia would oppose any deal that legitimizes Chinese hegemony in Asia.
    • Russia might see this as a U.S.-China condominium, leaving it out of the division.

  7. Economic Decoupling Trends

    • The U.S. and China are actively decoupling in tech (semiconductors, AI), finance (reserve currency), and military (dual-use exports).

Alternative (More Plausible) Scenarios

Instead of a formal spheres-of-influence agreement, we might see:

    • Proxy conflicts (Ukraine, Africa, Latin America) continue but at lower intensity.

  2. Regionalized Competition

    • Asia: China dominates East Asia; U.S. maintains alliances (Japan, Australia, Philippines).
    • Europe: U.S. focuses on NATO; China expands influence via BRI (but avoids direct conflict).
    • Middle East: U.S. and China compete indirectly (e.g., oil deals, arms sales) without direct war.

  3. Taiwan as the Flashpoint

    • The most likely breaking point—if China invades Taiwan, the U.S. would respond militarily, making any spheres deal impossible.

  4. Collapse of Globalization

    • If decoupling accelerates, the world could fragment into blocs (U.S.-led, China-led, EU-led), but this would increase conflict risk.

Conclusion: Why a Formal Spheres Deal is Unlikely (But Not Impossible in the Long Run)

  • Short-term (next 10 years): Too many ideological, alliance, and domestic political obstacles.

  • Most probable outcome: A Cold War-style stalemate with controlled competition, occasional crises, and no formal division—but with increasing risks of miscalculation.

Final Thought

While a formal spheres-of-influence agreement might seem like a rational solution to avoid war, the structural rivalry between the U.S. and China is too deep, and third-party actors (allies, neutral states) would resist. The more likely path is managed competition with periodic crises—unless one side (China) dominates decisively or the U.S. accepts a unipolar Asian order, which neither seems willing to do yet.
